--- title: "Black boxes and interpretable models" description: "An interpretable model can be read from its parts; a black box is read from outside. On the survey a GAM, read curve by curve, predicts new sites as well as a random forest, and the two draw the same shapes. A black box earns its place where inputs work in combination, inputs are raw, or prediction is the whole job." order: 3 categories: [interpretation, metrics] --- ## Some models can be read from their parts An **interpretable model** is one whose fitted parts can be read directly. Poisson regression gives each input a multiplier; a GAM, below, gives each input a curve; a small tree gives a few questions. A **black box**, such as a random forest of 500 trees, boosting or a neural network, predicts well but has no part that means anything alone. It is read from outside instead, with [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) and [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd). It is often said that readable models predict worse, so that a study must choose between understanding and accuracy. This page tests that on the survey, then reads the readable model's parts in plain words. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A GAM gives each input one smooth curve A **generalised additive model (GAM)** replaces each input's straight line in a linear model with a smooth curve, and adds the curves up as a linear model adds its terms. The shape is free, as in a forest, but each input keeps one curve, the same whatever the other inputs are, so the curves can be drawn and compared with what is known about the species. Each curve is built from short, smooth bumps spread along the input's range, each with a weight, and the weighted bumps add up to a curve of almost any shape. A penalty on bending, like the penalty in [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd), stops the curve chasing the noise; its weight is chosen from the data. ::: {.diagram} ![A GAM covers the input's range with short smooth bumps, weights them, and adds them up into a curve. A penalty on bending stops the curve chasing the noise; with bending made very costly the curve becomes a straight line.](img/gam.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Pieces, short smooth bumps: seven bell-shaped curves overlap along the input's range. Added up, a weight for each bump: the bumps, each scaled by its weight, are drawn dashed, and their sum is a solid curve that rises and falls with the data points. Penalty, each bend costs: three curves through the same points; a dashed curve with bends made cheap chases the noise, a dotted straight line is what bends made dear give, and the solid curve between them follows the rise and fall. The text says fitting chooses the weights and pays for every bend, and the data set the price. A note says the curves add up, so each input keeps one curve that can be drawn and read."} ::: ## Scoring models on the same folds measures what reading costs Whether a readable model costs accuracy is a question for the data, and cross-validation answers it. Every model is scored on the same folds, built from whole sites as in [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd), so a hard fold is hard for all of them and the scores can be compared fold by fold, the **paired comparison** of [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd). ::: {.diagram} ![Two ways to read a model, and one way to score it. An interpretable model is read from its parts, curves and levels that add up to the prediction. A black box is probed from outside by changing its inputs and watching the prediction. Both are scored on the same held-out sites.](img/reading-a-model.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Read the parts, an interpretable model: three small plots, a humped curve for input A, a falling line for input B and three bars for the levels of input C, joined by plus signs, equal the prediction. Probe from outside, a black box: a dark box labelled 500 trees with inputs A, B and C as arrows going in; the arrow for A is orange and marked change, and an orange arrow coming out is marked watch; the text says importance and partial dependence do this. Score both, the same held-out sites: a row of ten blocks with one green block marked held-out sites, and below it two bars of nearly equal length for the interpretable model and the black box, marked error on new sites. A note says that however a model is read, it shows what the model learned, and the data decide how far that describes the species."} ::: ## Worked example Four models are scored by ten-fold cross-validation by site on the whole survey, with the inputs of [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). Two are interpretable: Poisson regression, with a straight line for each input on the log scale, and a GAM, with a curve for depth and temperature. Two are black boxes: the random forest of [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd), and boosting with the settings of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). Predicting the average is the baseline. The GAM is then fitted to every station and read. ### Preparing the data The GAM here uses the negative binomial, which [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) showed gives honest intervals when counts spread more than Poisson expects. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) count_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = survey ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") # boosting and the average take numbers only number_recipe <- count_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) # s() asks mgcv for a smooth curve; nb() is the negative binomial smooth_terms <- abundance ~ s(depth_m) + s(temperature_c) + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season gam_model <- gen_additive_mod() |> set_engine("mgcv", family = mgcv::nb(), method = "REML") |> set_mode("regression") models <- list( "Predicting the average" = workflow(number_recipe, null_model(mode = "regression")), "Poisson regression" = workflow(count_recipe, poisson_reg()), "GAM" = workflow(count_recipe) |> add_model(gam_model, formula = smooth_terms), "Random forest" = workflow(count_recipe, rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression")), "Boosting" = workflow(number_recipe, boost_tree(trees = 300, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) |> set_mode("regression")) ) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor from sklearn.ensemble import (GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor) from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, GroupKFold from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import (OneHotEncoder, SplineTransformer, StandardScaler) from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() folds = list(GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123) .split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical # shape() turns depth and temperature into columns: themselves, or a set of # spline bumps def recipe(shape): def curved(column): steps = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("shape", shape), ("scale", StandardScaler())]) return (column, steps, [column]) return ColumnTransformer([ curved("depth_m"), curved("temperature_c"), ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) def with_recipe(model, shape="passthrough"): return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe(shape)), ("model", model)]) # scikit-learn has no GAM. Spline bumps with a ridge penalty come close; the # penalty's weight is chosen by five-fold cross-validation by site. gam = GridSearchCV( with_recipe(PoissonRegressor(max_iter=1000), SplineTransformer(n_knots=8)), {"model__alpha": 10.0 ** np.arange(-4, 1)}, cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=5), scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") models = { "Predicting the average": with_recipe(DummyRegressor()), "Poisson regression": with_recipe(PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000)), "GAM": gam, # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults "Random forest": with_recipe(RandomForestRegressor( n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)), "Boosting": with_recipe(GradientBoostingRegressor( n_estimators=300, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=123)), } def fit(model, data): # only the GAM's search over its penalty needs the sites extra = {"groups": data["site_id"]} if model is gam else {} return clone(model).fit(data[predictors], data["abundance"], **extra) ``` ::: ::: ### On new sites the GAM predicts as well as the black boxes Each model is fitted ten times, each time leaving out one fold of sites, and scored on the sites it left out. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- imap(models, \(model, name) { fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) |> collect_metrics(summarize = FALSE) |> transmute(fold = id, model = name, rmse = .estimate) }) |> list_rbind() kind <- c("Predicting the average" = "Baseline", "Poisson regression" = "Interpretable", "GAM" = "Interpretable", "Random forest" = "Black box", "Boosting" = "Black box") # each fold's RMSE beside the average's and the GAM's on the same fold by_fold <- scores |> left_join(scores |> filter(model == "Predicting the average") |> select(fold, average = rmse), by = "fold") |> left_join(scores |> filter(model == "GAM") |> select(fold, gam = rmse), by = "fold") comparison <- by_fold |> summarise(RMSE = mean(rmse), `Folds better than the average` = sum(rmse < average), `Folds better than the GAM` = sum(rmse < gam), .by = model) |> mutate(Kind = kind[model], .after = model) |> rename(Model = model) comparison |> mutate(RMSE = round(RMSE, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model |Kind | RMSE| Folds better than the average| Folds better than the GAM| |:----------------------|:-------------|----:|-----------------------------:|-------------------------:| |Predicting the average |Baseline | 4.62| 0| 1| |Poisson regression |Interpretable | 4.50| 7| 0| |GAM |Interpretable | 4.34| 9| 0| |Random forest |Black box | 4.43| 8| 1| |Boosting |Black box | 4.53| 7| 1|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rows = [] for fold, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(folds, start=1): fitting, held = survey.iloc[fit_rows], survey.iloc[held_rows] for name, model in models.items(): predicted = fit(model, fitting).predict(held[predictors]) rows.append({"fold": fold, "model": name, "rmse": root_mean_squared_error(held["abundance"], predicted)}) # one row per fold, one column per model by_fold = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="fold", columns="model", values="rmse")[list(models)] kind = {"Predicting the average": "Baseline", "Poisson regression": "Interpretable", "GAM": "Interpretable", "Random forest": "Black box", "Boosting": "Black box"} pd.DataFrame({ "Kind": kind, "RMSE": by_fold.mean().round(2), "Folds better than the average": by_fold.lt(by_fold["Predicting the average"], axis=0).sum(), "Folds better than the GAM": by_fold.lt(by_fold["GAM"], axis=0).sum(), }).rename_axis("Model").reset_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Model | Kind | RMSE | Folds better than the average | Folds better than the GAM | |:-----------------------|:--------------|-------:|--------------------------------:|----------------------------:| | Predicting the average | Baseline | 4.71 | 0 | 0 | | Poisson regression | Interpretable | 4.28 | 10 | 3 | | GAM | Interpretable | 4.13 | 10 | 0 | | Random forest | Black box | 4.26 | 10 | 2 | | Boosting | Black box | 4.65 | 8 | 1 | ::: ::: ::: The GAM, an interpretable model, has the lowest RMSE on new sites, 4.34 individuals against 4.43 for the random forest and 4.62 for predicting the average. Fold by fold the forest beats it on only 1 of the 10 folds, and boosting on 1. Boosting is the weakest of the four, at 4.53; it is untuned here, and [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) would narrow the gap. Every model is only a little better than the average. The GAM's error moves from 3.48 to 6.94 between folds, far more than it differs between models: which sites are left out matters more than which model is used. The counts are noisy, and no model predicts one catch closely. The readable model costs nothing here because the survey's effects are of the kind a GAM assumes: smooth curves, one for each input, that add up. Where the effects are like that, a GAM loses nothing to a forest and can be read. ### The GAM's curves read as a habitat description A GAM's parts are curves and multipliers, and each can be put in words. The curves for depth and temperature are drawn with their 95% intervals, each relative to its peak, over the middle 90% of each input as in [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd). The forest's partial dependence is drawn beside them, the same shape read from outside a black box. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gam_fit <- fit(models[["GAM"]], survey) forest_fit <- fit(models[["Random forest"]], survey) gam_engine <- extract_fit_engine(gam_fit) prepared <- extract_recipe(gam_fit) along <- function(input) { values <- quantile(survey[[input]], c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) levels <- seq(values[1], values[2], length.out = 40) # the GAM's own curve for the input and its interval; on the log scale it # adds the same amount at every station, so its shape is the same at all grid <- survey[rep(1, 40), ] grid[[input]] <- levels term <- predict(gam_engine, bake(prepared, grid), type = "terms", se.fit = TRUE) curve <- term$fit[, paste0("s(", input, ")")] spread <- 1.96 * term$se.fit[, paste0("s(", input, ")")] gam_curve <- tibble(value = levels, .pred = exp(curve - max(curve)), lower = exp(curve - spread - max(curve)), upper = exp(curve + spread - max(curve))) forest_curve <- map(levels, \(level) { swept <- survey swept[[input]] <- level tibble(value = level, .pred = mean(predict(forest_fit, swept)$.pred)) }) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(.pred = .pred / max(.pred)) bind_rows(GAM = gam_curve, "Random forest" = forest_curve, .id = "model") } curves <- map(c(depth_m = "depth_m", temperature_c = "temperature_c"), along) curve_plot <- function(input, x_label) { ggplot(curves[[input]], aes(value, .pred, colour = model)) + # only the GAM has an interval geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), data = \(d) filter(d, model == "GAM"), fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(GAM = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Random forest" = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + labs(x = x_label, y = "Count relative to its peak", colour = NULL) } curve_plot("depth_m", "Depth (m)") + curve_plot("temperature_c", "Temperature (°C)") + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The GAM's curves for depth and temperature with their 95% intervals, against the random forest's partial dependence, each relative to its peak. Temperature: both peak in cool water and fall on either side, the GAM's more steeply. Depth: both are highest in the shallowest water and fall with depth.](black-box-or-not_files/figure-html/fig-gam-curves-1.png){#fig-gam-curves fig-alt='Two panels, depth on the left and temperature on the right, each with a blue GAM curve inside a shaded blue interval and an orange random forest curve, scaled so each peaks at 1. Depth: both curves are highest at the shallowest depth drawn and fall towards the deepest; the GAM\'s falls further, and its interval is widest in the shallowest water. Temperature: both curves are humps that peak in cool water, the GAM\'s narrower and falling lower at both ends than the forest\'s, with an interval that widens towards both ends.' width=1900} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} gam_fit = fit(gam, survey) forest_fit = fit(models["Random forest"], survey) # a GAM's curve has the same shape at every station, so one station shows it typical = survey[numeric].median() def along(column): swept = partial_dependence(forest_fit, survey[predictors], [column], percentiles=(0.05, 0.95), grid_resolution=40) levels = swept["grid_values"][0] grid = pd.DataFrame({c: [typical[c]] * len(levels) for c in numeric}) grid[column] = levels grid["substrate"], grid["season"] = "sand", "summer" gam_curve = gam_fit.predict(grid[predictors]) forest_curve = swept["average"][0] return pd.DataFrame({"value": levels, "GAM": gam_curve / gam_curve.max(), "Random forest": forest_curve / forest_curve.max()}) curves = {column: along(column) for column in ["depth_m", "temperature_c"]} # where each curve peaks, and how low it falls at either end pd.DataFrame([ {"Input": column, "Model": model, "Peak": curve.loc[curve[model].idxmax(), "value"], "At the low end": curve[model].iloc[0], "At the high end": curve[model].iloc[-1]} for column, curve in curves.items() for model in ["GAM", "Random forest"] ]).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Input | Model | Peak | At the low end | At the high end | |:--------------|:--------------|-------:|-----------------:|------------------:| | depth_m | GAM | 25.91 | 1 | 0.29 | | depth_m | Random forest | 36 | 0.99 | 0.59 | | temperature_c | GAM | 8.06 | 0.23 | 0.2 | | temperature_c | Random forest | 7.81 | 0.56 | 0.6 | ::: ::: ::: In words, from the GAM: - **Temperature.** The count peaks near 7.7 °C. It falls to 25% of the peak at 4.1 °C and to 15% at 13.5 °C, the coldest and warmest water drawn. The interval is narrow through the middle and widens at the ends, where there are fewer stations. - **Depth.** The count is highest at the shallowest stations and falls to 25% of that by 157 m. [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) showed that this curve follows position, since the shelf deepens offshore, and the GAM inherits the same confounding. Its interval shows how closely the data pin the curve down, not whether it is the species' response to depth. The forest, read from outside, draws the same shapes: its temperature curve peaks near 7.7 °C and its depth curve is also highest in the shallowest water. It is flatter at the ends, as forests are where stations thin out. Two models that work in different ways agree, which says the shapes are in the data. The other inputs have one multiplier each, read as in [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} multipliers <- tidy(extract_fit_engine(gam_fit), parametric = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> transmute(term = str_replace(term, "^(substrate|season)", "\\1: "), multiplier = estimate, conf_low = conf.low, conf_high = conf.high) multipliers |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | multiplier| conf_low| conf_high| |:-----------------|----------:|--------:|---------:| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.12| 1.06| 1.20| |salinity_psu | 1.07| 0.85| 1.35| |substrate: gravel | 1.21| 0.99| 1.49| |substrate: mud | 1.44| 1.22| 1.71| |substrate: rock | 0.80| 0.59| 1.09| |season: summer | 1.66| 1.11| 2.47| |season: autumn | 1.17| 0.93| 1.49| |season: winter | 0.83| 0.59| 1.17|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # scikit-learn gives no intervals. Its chlorophyll and salinity were scaled, # so their coefficients are divided by the scale to give one unit's change. best = gam_fit.best_estimator_ names = best["recipe"].get_feature_names_out() coefficients = pd.Series(best["model"].coef_, index=names) scale = best["recipe"].named_transformers_["numeric"]["scale"].scale_ coefficients[["numeric__chlorophyll_mg_m3", "numeric__salinity_psu"]] /= scale kept = coefficients[~coefficients.index.str.contains("depth|temperature")] pd.DataFrame({ "term": kept.index.str.replace(r"^numeric__", "", regex=True) .str.replace(r"^categorical__(substrate|season)_", r"\1: ", regex=True), "multiplier": np.exp(kept).round(2).to_numpy(), }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | multiplier | |:------------------|-------------:| | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.12 | | salinity_psu | 1.05 | | substrate: gravel | 1.12 | | substrate: mud | 1.34 | | substrate: rock | 0.81 | | season: autumn | 1.08 | | season: summer | 1.25 | | season: winter | 0.9 | ::: ::: ::: - **Substrate.** A muddy station is expected to hold 1.44 times the count of a sandy one, with an interval from 1.22 to 1.71. Rock's interval, 0.59 to 1.09, includes 1: the data cannot tell rock from sand. - **Season.** Summer holds 1.66 times the count of spring. - **Chlorophyll.** Each extra mg/m³ multiplies the count by 1.12. - **Salinity.** Its interval, 0.85 to 1.35, includes 1, so the survey cannot say whether salinity raises or lowers the count. Each multiplier comes with its interval, and an interval that includes 1 says plainly that the data cannot answer. Getting the same from a forest takes a partial dependence plot for every input, with no interval attached. ## A black box earns its place where inputs work in combination A GAM's curves add up, so it cannot show an effect of one input that depends on another. A black box can, and it earns its place in three kinds of work. - **Inputs that work in combination.** A water mass is a diagonal band in temperature and salinity. In [When a network pays off](../09-neural-networks/when-a-network-pays-off.qmd) a network draws it from a few hundred stations, while logistic regression matches it only once the combination is named as an input. A black box well ahead of a GAM is a sign of such a combination, worth finding and naming. - **Raw inputs.** Images, sound and spectra have no input whose curve means anything alone, so there is nothing to give up by using a black box. - **Prediction as the whole job.** An operational forecast or a tool to plan survey effort is judged by its predictions. A readable model fitted beside it remains a useful check. Fitting both and scoring them on the same folds, as here, shows which case a study is in. Where the readable model is close, report it and read it; where the black box is well ahead, it has found structure the readable one is missing. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - An **interpretable model** is read from its parts: a GAM's curves, a Poisson regression's multipliers. A **black box** is read from outside, with feature importance and partial dependence. - Scored on the same folds of sites, the GAM predicted new sites as well as the random forest and better than boosting: on the survey, reading cost no accuracy. - The GAM's parts read as a habitat description, each with an interval: a temperature peak in cool water, more animals on mud than on sand, and no answer on salinity. - The GAM and the forest drew the same shapes. Agreement says the shape is in the data, not that it is the species' response: both depth curves follow position. - A black box earns its place where inputs work in combination, where inputs are raw, or where prediction is the whole job. A black box well ahead of a readable model points to structure worth naming. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Give chlorophyll a curve as well, with `s(chlorophyll_mg_m3)` in `smooth_terms`, and score the GAM again. Does its RMSE change, and what shape does the new curve have? 2. Tune boosting's `trees`, `tree_depth` and `learn_rate` with `tune_grid()` on the same folds, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). Does it overtake the GAM?
